To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is a substantial heterogeneity in the level of sequential innovation across industries, (2) sequentiality is a key determinant of firm dynamics and patent policy, and (3) patent policy can improve welfare in sequential industries.
there is substantial heterogeneity in the sequential nature of innovation across industries and that patent policy should account for this heterogeneity.

the level of sequential interdependence across industries is positively associated with: (a) the rate of innovation, (b) the variance of growth rates, (c) the rate of exit, (d) the profitability of firms, (e) the rate of patent expiry, (f) the degree of patent thickets and (g) the level of misallocation of resources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of patent policy in the innovation process.
the relationship between the structure of the innovation process and the design of patent policy.
the impact of interdependence on the dynamics of innovation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
The patent policy should be more lenient for the industries with higher sequentiality index, which is a measure of interdependence between old and new technologies in the industry.
the results of the thesis are in accordance with the theory and the empirical evidence.
the results of the model and the empirical analysis suggest that the patent system is an effective mechanism to encourage innovation and the diffusion of technology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we develop an industry level measure of sequentiality, which is a measure of how new technologies are related to existing technologies in an industry, and we use this measure to study the implications of patent policy for innovation and growth.
we have constructed a measure of interdependence between technologies in different industries.
the patent system is a good way to incentivize innovation, but that it has a few flaws that can be addressed by policy changes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patent protection should be weaker in more sequential industries.
the patent policy should be more aggressive in industries where new innovations are more likely to be based on previous innovations (sequential industries).
the sequentiality in the development of new technologies has a significant impact on firm dynamics.
